original_question: Let S be a semi-algebraic subset of R^k defined by s polynomial equalities and inequalities whose degrees are bounded by d. Is there an algorithm that computes all Betti numbers of S in time single exponential in k? More concretely, can the currently known single-exponential methods for computing only the first l Betti numbers for fixed l be extended to compute the full Betti sequence of S within a single-exponential running time in the ambient dimension?
target_in_paper: Section 9, unnumbered open problem "Computing Betti Numbers in Single Exponential Time ?"
correct_elements: Your draft captures the right open problem: the paper asks whether one can compute all Betti numbers of a semi-algebraic set in single-exponential time in the ambient dimension k, and it correctly contrasts this with the known result that for each fixed ell one can compute only the first ell+1 Betti numbers in singly exponential time. This is exactly the gap highlighted between Theorem 6.10 and the open problem in Section 9.
missing_details: The paper formulates the problem over a real closed field R, not just over the field of real numbers.

The input set is an arbitrary P-semi-algebraic set defined by a Boolean formula with atoms P = 0, P > 0, or P < 0 for P in a finite family P subset R[X1,...,Xk]; saying only 'defined by s polynomial equalities and inequalities' can be read too narrowly as a basic conjunction.
The parameters should be named exactly: s = #(P) and d = max_{P in P} deg(P).
The Betti numbers in the paper are b_i(S) = dim_Q H^i(S,Q), i.e. cohomology with rational coefficients.
The complexity model should be stated: arithmetic operations and comparisons in the ordered ring generated by the input coefficients (Definition 2.2), not an unspecified Turing-style running time.
The paper's notion of 'single exponential in k' is the standard semi-algebraic-geometry one, namely complexity of the form (sd)^{k^{O(1)}} rather than double exponential in k.
The currently known result should be stated precisely: for any fixed ell, Theorem 6.10 computes b_0(S),...,b_ell(S) with complexity (sd)^{k^{O(ell)}}.

The paper's official formulation is an existence question ('does there exist such an algorithm?'), not primarily a question about whether the presently known methods must themselves extend, even though the paper remarks that extending those ideas is a major challenge.
To be fully stand-alone, 'all Betti numbers' should be made explicit as the full sequence b_0(S),...,b_k(S) for S subset R^k.
No homogeneity, nilpotency, or 'for all sufficiently large m' hypothesis occurs here; a paper-faithful rewrite should make clear that no such extra restrictions are part of the question.
refined_question: Let R be a real closed field, let P subset R[X1,...,Xk] be a finite family of polynomials with s = #(P) and d = max_{P in P} deg(P), and let S subset R^k be the P-semi-algebraic set defined by an arbitrary Boolean formula with atoms P = 0, P > 0, or P < 0. Is there an algorithm, measured in the arithmetic-complexity model of Definition 2.2, whose complexity is single exponential in k (that is, bounded by (sd)^{k^{O(1)}}), which computes the full Betti sequence b_0(S),...,b_k(S), where b_i(S) = dim_Q H^i(S,Q)? Equivalently, can the fixed-ell result of Theorem 6.10, which computes b_0(S),...,b_ell(S) in time (sd)^{k^{O(ell)}}, be strengthened to a single-exponential algorithm for all Betti numbers of an arbitrary semi-algebraic set?
justification: The draft is aiming at the paper's unnumbered Section 9 open problem 'Computing Betti Numbers in Single Exponential Time ?', stated on page 69. The exact nearby context needed to sharpen it is: Section 2.1, which defines P-semi-algebraic sets and the Betti numbers b_i(S) as dimensions of cohomology groups with rational coefficients; Definition 2.2 together with the subsequent discussion in Section 2.3, which explains the complexity model and the meaning of 'single exponential'; and Theorem 6.10 in Section 6.3.3, which is the precise currently known result for the first ell+1 Betti numbers. Your draft is already very close, but it should be broadened from basic equalities/inequalities over R to arbitrary Boolean P-formulas over a real closed field, and sharpened from an 'extension of current methods' phrasing to the paper's official existence question.
